top_choice_rationale: P001 (Chetty, Hendren, Friedman) credits a new empirical object, population-scale administrative measurement of intergenerational mobility, together with mover and childhood-exposure designs that separate place effects from family sorting. Outside researchers can check these designs directly, and they have already been used with other national registers. The attribution is the tightest on the slate, though the Friedman/Katz seat is a real judgement. Maturity is the main cost, since the core work dates from about 2014 to 2022. A citation limited to measurement and exposure-based designs, with no claim about long-run causal effects or policy conclusions, rests on what is best established. P003 is second because of its maturity and concentrated credit, despite weaker cross-country identification and its timing proximity to the 2024 prize. P002 (Kiyotaki-Moore) is third: it has a clean attribution but mostly indirect aggregate evidence and overlaps with the 2022 prize. P004 is fourth because a three-name cut of an eight-name field cannot be defended on a principled criterion. No award is last, since each of the four proposals recognises substantive, prize-level work.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; my frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited on any proposal. I disclose that my work with administrative data and quasi-experimental designs is adjacent to P001 and may bias me toward design-based evidence.
